AVALON CITY COUNCIL MEETING
  TUESDAY, JUNE 6, 2023 - 4:30 P.M.
  410 AVALON CANYON ROAD
  THIS VIRTUAL MEETING IS HELD PURSUANT TO AB 361
  AGENDA

  In compliance with the Americans with Disability Act, if you need special assistance to participate in this
  meeting, please contact the City Clerk's Office (310) 510-0220. Notification 48 hours prior to the meeting will
  enable the City to make reasonable arrangements to ensure accessibility to this meeting. (28 CFR 35. 102-
  35.104 ADA Title II). All public records relating to an agenda item on this agenda are available for the public
  inspection at the time the records are distributed to all, or a majority of all, members of the City Council. Such
  records shall be available at City Hall located at 410 Avalon Canyon Rd.

Due to social distancing recommendations from the Center for Disease Control and State of
California Division of Occupational Safety and Health (Cal/OSHA) and the County of Los
Angeles, and pursuant to findings made under AB 361, the CITY OF AVALON'S CITY COUNCIL
SHALL GENERALLY BE AVAILABLE TO THE PUBLIC REMOTELY. The general public may
attend the meeting in the Council Chambers however must adhere to social distancing
requirements. The public is encouraged to watch and participate from the safety of their homes
while practicing social distancing.

Council Chambers are open to a maximum 30 members of the general public. Once the Council
Chambers reach maximum occupancy, the general public may participate in Oral
Communication and address the City Council on an agenda item in person by waiting in the City
Hall Court Yard and entering the Chambers one at a time at the appropriate time. No one will be
admitted into the Council Chambers who is ill or exhibiting symptoms of COVID-19. Additionally,
the general public may participate in Oral Communication and address the City Council on an
agenda items by providing comments via Zoom or by sending comments to
ask@cityofavalon.com.

  For the public's convenience, but not participation, the meeting can be viewed:
  On local cable: Catalina Broadband Solutions channel 3
  Streaming Online: www.cityofavalon.com/meetings
  *Streaming on Facebook Live: www.facebook.com/CityOfAvalonOfficial
  Streaming on YouTube: https://www.youtube.com/CityofAvalonCA

FOR REMOTE PUBLIC PARTICIPATION
1) Join the Meeting via Phone Conference (Voice Only):
  Phone Number: (669) 444-9171,
  Meeting ID: 865 4733 0775
  Passcode: 064959

When you would like to comment during the meeting enter *9 on the phone's key pad to
activate the "raise hand" button at the time the Agenda Item is being presented for City Council
consideration.

3.  Findings to Continue to Hold Remote TeleconferenceNirtual City Council Meetings
  Pursuant to Assembly Bill 361
  As the State of Emergency has ended, the City Council can continue to hold virtual
  meetings without providing notice of the City Council's teleconference location if the City
  Council m~kes the following two findings: 1. State or local officials have imposed or
  recommended measures to promote social distancing in connection with COVID-19; and
  2. The City Council reconsiders the circumstances of the state of the emergency and
  danger presented by COVID-19; Having made the findings , the City Council can continue
  every 30 days to authorize meetings under AB 261 to protect the health or safety of
  attendees.
  Recommended Action
  Reconsider the circumstances of COVID-19 state of emergency proclaimed by the
  Governor and COVID-19's continued impact and determine that state or local officials
  have imposed or recommended measures to promote social distancing in connection with
  COVID-19, and as such, that continuing to utilize the protections of Assembly Bill 361 will
  protect the health and safely of attendees.

4.  Cooperation Agreement for Continued Participation in the Los Angeles Urban County
  Community Development Block Grant Program
  The City of Avalon receives Community Development Block Grant Funding annually
  through an agreement with The Los Angeles County Development Authority. The current
  agreement expires on July 1, 2023.
  Recommended Action
  Authorize the City Manager to execute the cooperation agreement with the Los Angeles
  County Development Authority for a three-year term beginning July1 , 2023 - June 30,
  2027.

5.  Resolution Adopting List of Projects for Annual SB1 Allocation
  Senate Bill 1 provides funding to address basic road maintenance, rehabilitation and
  critical safety needs of local streets and roads in addition for other transportation needs
  in the state. One of the requirements of the program is that each agency must adopt a list
  of projects for their annual formula allocation that is submitted to the California
  Transportation Commission.
  Recommended Action
  Adopt a resolution adopting a project for Fiscal Year 2023-24 funded by S81 : The Road
  Repair and Accountability Act of 2017.

PUBLIC HEARING

6.  Fiscal Year 2023-2024 Miscellaneous Fee Schedule
  The City charges fees for miscellaneous public services, use of City facilities and
  equipment rental and other activities. User fees are assessed and collected for City
  services and programs provided by various departments.
 CITY COUNCIL AGENDA
JUNE 6, 2023
PAGE4

  Recommended Action
  1. Hear a presentation regarding the Miscellaneous Fee Schedule. 2. Open the Public
  Hearing to hear public comments. 3. Close the Public Hearing . 4. If consensus, adopt
  the fee schedule as proposed.

7.  Public Hearing Regarding Resolutions Adopting the Reports Proposing to Have Sewer,
  Saltwater, and Solid Waste Collection Service, and Grease Collection Service Charges
  Collected on the Property Tax Roll for Fiscal Year 2023-24 and Directing the City Clerk
  to File Said Report with the Los Angeles Auditor-Controller to Place Said Charges on the
  Tax Roll
  In order for Los Angeles County to collect the Charges for the City on the property tax
  roll, the City Council is required to hold a noticed public hearing, where customers subject
  to the fees are afforded an opportunity to make objections or protests to collecting the
  fees on the property tax roll.
  Recommended Action
  1. Open a public hearing on whether to collect the annual solid waste collection service
  charges, grease collection service charges, sewer charges, and saltwater charges
  (collectively, the "Charges"), on the property tax roll by the County of Los Angeles. 2. If
  no majority protest is filed, close the public hearing and adopt four resolution adopting
  reports of the Charges.

8.  TOA Article 8 Hearing
  The Metropolitan Transit Authority (MTA) is required to hold a public hearing on the
  community's unmet public transit needs in accordance with the Transportation
  Development Act (TOA) Article 8. TOA Article 8 funds are currently being used by the
  City of Avalon to fund Avalon's Consolidated Land Transportation Program which
  includes DAR and fixed routes.
  Recommended Action
  Open the Public Hearing and accept comments from the public. Close the Public Hearing.

GENERAL BUSINESS

9.  Contract Assignment for Semi-Exclusive Shore Boat Franchise and Shore Boat Services
  Provider Agreement
  This item appears on the agenda at the request of representatives from Catalina Coastal
  Tours, LLC. The City Council considered a request from Catalina Coastal Tours, LLC to
  assign the remaining term of the semi-exclusive shore boat franchise agreement to
  Catalina Coastal Shoreboat Service, LLC. The City Council requested the potential
  assignee provide additional information. No additional information was provided.
  Recommended Action
  Consider a request to assign the remaining term of the semi-exclusive shore boat
  franchise agreement with Catalina Coastal Tours, LLC to Catalina Coastal Shoreboat
  Service, LLC. Provide direction to Staff.

SUBJECT:  Findings to Continue to Hold Remote TeleconferenceNirtual City
  Council Meetings Pursuant to Assembly Bill 361

RECOMMENDED ACTION(S): Reconsider the circumstances of COVID-19 state of emergency
proclaimed by the Governor and COVID-19's continued impact and determine that state or local
officials have imposed or recommended measures to promote social distancing in connection
with COVID-19, and as such, that continuing to utilize the protections of Assembly Bill 361 will
protect the health and safely of attendees.

REPORT SUMMARY: Traditionally, the Brown Act allows for teleconference or virtual meetings,
provided that the physical locations of the legislative body's members joining by teleconference
are posted on the agenda, that those locations are open to the public and that a quorum of the
members is located within its jurisdiction. AB 361 provides an exceptio~ to these procedures in
order to allow for fully virtual meetings during proclaimed emergencies, including the COVID-19
pandemic.

Since March of 2020 and the issuance of Governor Newsom's Executive Order N-29-20, which
suspended portions of the Brown Act relating to teleconferencing, the City Council has had virtual
meetings without having to post the location of the legislative body members attending virtually.
Most public agencies have been holding public meetings using virtual platforms since this time.
In June of 2021, Governor Newsom issued Executive Order N-08-21, which provided that the
exceptions contained in EO N-29-20 would sunset on September 30, 2021.

On September 10, 2021, the Legislature adopted AB 361, which allows public agencies to hold
fully virtual meetings under certain circumstances without the posting of the agenda from each
location a legislative body member is attending. Governor Newsom signed the bill into law on
September 16, 2021 . Because it contained an urgency provision, it took immediate effect.

Specific Findings Required under AB 361

As the State of Emergency has ended, the City Council can continue to hold virtual meetings
without providing notice of the City Council's teleconference location if the City Council makes
the following two findings :

  1. State or local officials have imposed or recommended measures to promote social
  distancing in connection with COVID-19; and

  2. The City Council reconsiders the circumstances of the state of the emergency and danger
  presented by COVID-19;
65059.00000\3452048 I. I
 Having made the findings, the City Council can continue every 30 days to authorize meetings
under AB 261 to protect the health or safety of attendees.

COVI D-19 continues to present a threat to the health or safety of members of the public. Although
vaccines are now widely available, many people in the State and County are still not fully
vaccinated and remain susceptible to infection. The disease can still spread rapidly through
person-to-person contact and those in close proximity. According to the most recently published
data, , 5.5% of those tested statewide for COVID-19 tested positive, an increase of 1.0% from
the prior week. In Los Angeles County, there are 272 patients hospitalized with COVID-19 and
an average of 4 deaths per day and hundreds of people are hospitalized with COVID-19.
Additionally, Cal/OHSA has implemented COVID-19 Prevention Non-Emergency Regulations
that will remain in effect until February 3, 2025. The City's economy is dependent upon visitors
to the island, the presence of which , increases the likelihood of transmission of the disease. Also,
having members of the public attend council meetings at locations where council members are
in attendance due to their desire to avoid exposure to COVI D-19 poses a risk to the health or
safety of attendees.

Re-Authorization is Required Within 30 Days

The City Council made the required findings at its May 16, 2023 City Council meeting. Consistent
with the provisions of AB 361, the new findings must be made every 30 days. Thus, if the City
Council desires to continue to meet remotely without having to post the location of each
teleconference location, the City Council reconsider the facts of the state of emergency and
continued impact of COVID-19, find that state or local officials have imposed or recommended
measures to promote social distancing in connection with COVID-19, and therefore, that remote
meetings under AB 361 should continue in order to protect the health or safety of attendees.

CONSEQUENCES OF NOT FOLLOWING RECOMMENDED ACTION: The City Council will
have to follow the Brown Act provisions that existed prior to the COVID-19 pandemic.

FOLLOW UP ACTION: That the City Council make the findings under AB 361 at its June 20,
2023 City Council meeting.

SUBJECT:  Resolution Adopting List of Projects for Annual SB1 Allocation

RECOMMENDED ACTION(S): Adopt a resolution adopting a project for Fiscal Year 2023-24
funded by SB1: The Road Repair and Accountability Act of 2017.

REPORT SUMMARY: In 201 7 Senate Bill 1 (SB1) was enacted, and provided new funding to
address basic road maintenance, rehabilitation and critical safety needs of local streets and
roads in addition for other transportation needs in the state.

One of the requirements of the program is that each agency must adopt a list of projects for
their annual formula allocation that is submitted to the California Transportation Commission .

The City's estimated allocation for the upcoming Fiscal Year 2023-24 is $83,454. Staff
identified the Five Corners Complete Street Project, known as the City of Avalon Five Corner
Comprehensive Pedestrian Project as the project that would provide the greatest benefit for
the community with the upcoming fiscal year allocation. This determination was based on the
City's need to provide matching funds to the existing grant funds.

GOAL ALIGNMENT: N/A

FISCAL IMPACTS: The addition of $83,454 to Account No.10575-6547.

CONSEQUENCES OF NOT FOLLOWING RECOMMENDED ACTION: The City would not
receive allocations of SB1 funds.

FOLLOW UP ACTION: Submit the approved project list and resolution to the California
Transportation Commission through the CalSMART system by July 1, 2023.

ADVERTISING, NOTICE AND PUBLIC CONTACT: This item was properly listed on the
posted agenda pursuant to the Brown Act.

SUBJECT:  Fiscal Year 2023-2024 Miscellaneous Fee Schedule

RECOMMENDED ACTION($): 1. Hear a presentation regarding the Miscellaneous Fee
Schedule. 2. Open the Public Hearing to hear public comments. 3. Close the Public Hearing. 4.
If consensus, adopt the fee schedule as proposed.

REPORT SUMMARY: The City charges fees for miscellaneous public services, use of City
facilities and ·equipment rental and other activities. User fees are assessed and collected for City
services and programs provided by various departments. These are services that convey a
benefit, grant a privilege, provide for review and enforcement of regulatory activities, enforce
laws, or are a condition of development. Under State law, cities may charge fees to recoup the
direct and indirect costs related to the provision of user services.

Each year, the City reviews its fees to establish new fees, modify existing fees, and eliminate
fees that are no longer required to ensure that City fees are in-line with the costs incurred to
provide them. The City made a number of edits to the prior year's fee schedule to better organize
the grouping of fees. For example, the rental of City Hall Council Chambers has been moved
from the Administration section to the Facility Rentals section of the document and a new section ·
was created for vehicle-related fees.

In Fiscal Year 2022-2023, City Council approved a 5.07% increase for the majority of fees, with
the exception of transit and certain recreation fees. The percentage increase was based on the
consumer price index (CPI) information provided by the Bureau of Labor Statistics for Los
Angeles County based on the latest available fiscal year information. Using the CPI as an
average cost increase annually ensures the city does not unnecessarily burden the citizens with
unusually large spikes in fees while also ensuring that the City continues to recoup costs
associated with the increased costs to provide these services.

For Fiscal Year 2023-2024, Staff recommends increasing the majority of fees based on the latest
available calendar year consumer price index (CPI) _information provided by the Bureau of Labor
Statistics for Los Angeles County which shows an increase of 3.82% based for the twelve
months ending April 2023, with the fees rounded to the nearest dollar.

As part of its review process, the City elected to not increase certain fees related to recreation
and transit, with those services to be subsidized with general tax revenues. The City also
reduced its annual dog license fee to encourage greater participation in the program. In addition,
 the City changed its tiered discount for facility rentals from a five-tiered system to a three-tiered
system to simplify the discount process for members of the public and Staff, as summarized
below:

  •  Group 1 = City of Avalon sponsored or co-sponsored event or program; No rental fee
  •  Group 2 = Resident private use, not-for-profit organizations, and governmental agencies
  eligible for fee discount
  •  Group 3 = Non-resident private use and commercial use not eligible for discount

Lastly, Staff has identified several fees which did not fully capture the cost for providing these
services and increased the fee by more than CPI, including the film license application fee, which
increased from $27 to $150 per application, the various vehicle renewal fees , which increased
from $37 to $50 per vehicle.

The proposed fee schedule has been available for public review and inspection for at least 10
days.

GOAL ALIGNMENT: City costs will be offset by annual revenues.

FISCAL IMPACTS: Staff estimates that the new City fees, if adopted as proposed, should
generate approximately $120,000 in the General Fund and $100,000 in Harbor Fund revenues.

CONSEQUENCES OF NOT FOLLOWING RECOMMENDED ACTION: The costs of special
services will not be fully funded through fees paid by the users of those services. The unfunded
portion of user services would then be subsidized by° general tax revenues and/or available fund
balances.

FOLLOW UP ACTION:  Adopt the attached resolution establishing city rates and fees for
services.

SUBJECT:  Public Hearing Regarding Resolutions Adopting the Reports
  Proposing to Have Sewer, Saltwater, and Solid Waste Collection
  Service, and Grease Collection Service Charges Collected on the
  Property Tax Roll for Fiscal Year 2023-24 and Directing the City
  Clerk to File Said Report with the Los Angeles Auditor-Controller to
  Place Said Charges on the Tax Roll

RECOMMENDED ACTION(S): 1. Open a public hearing on whether to collect the annual
solid waste collection service charges, grease collection service charges, sewer charges, and
saltwater charges (collectively, the "Charges"), on the property tax roll by the County of Los
Angeles. 2. If no majority protest is filed, close the public hearing and adopt four resolution
adopting reports of the Charges.

REPORT SUMMARY: In order for Los Angeles County to collect the Charges for the City on
the property tax roll, the City Council is required to hold a noticed public hearing, where
customers subject to the fees are afforded an opportunity to make objections or protests to
collecting the fees on the property tax roll. If objections or protests are not made by the
owners of a majority of the separate parcels subject to the fees, the City Council may adopt the
reports of the annual fees and direct the City Clerk to file the reports with the Los Angeles
County Auditor and request the fees be placed on the County property tax roll. Collecting the
fees on the property tax rolls saves the City the costs of billing the Charges itself. The County
charges approximately $0.25 per fee per parcel.

On June 1, 2021, the City Council approved a five-year schedule of rates for the Charges. City
Staff is proposing the following rates for the Fiscal Year 2023-2024, which are less than the
previously approved rates, as follows:

  •  Sewer +3.5%
  •  Saltwater +2.5%
  •  Solid Waste +7.5%
  •  Grease Collection +7.5%

The increases are necessary to adequately fund capital improvements to existing infrastructure
and to develop and maintain adequate reserve levels. In particular, the Solid Waste fund
proposed rate increases reflect additional revenues required to fund new state recycling
mandates, permitting for potential landfill expansion, and contributions to landfill trust fund for -
future closure and post-closure costs. The rate increase for Sewer and Saltwater services are
aligned with the rates included in the adopted study. The adopted study had included a 19.5%
 increase for Solid Waste and Grease Collection rates for Fiscal Year 2023-24 and a 9.5%
increase for Fiscal Year 2023-24. However, due to delayed expenditures related to landfill
expansion, the City has been able to more gradually phase the required increases of 11.5% for
Fiscal Year 2022-2023 and a proposed 7.5% for Fiscal Year 2023-2024. A copy of the current
and proposed fees based on customer classification has been included as an attachment to
this report.

GOAL ALIGNMENT: Achieve a structurally balanced budget by generating more revenue
through the efficient collection of Charges on the property tax roll.

FISCAL IMPACTS: The rates published in the proposed rate schedule attached will increase
the total Sewer revenue by approximately $100,000 next year; increase the total Saltwater
revenue by approximately $20,000 next year, and increase the Solid Waste revenue by
$185,000 next year.

CONSEQUENCES OF NOT FOLLOWING RECOMMENDED ACTION: If the Charges are not
placed on the property tax roll, the City would have to directly bill property owners and
customers for those Charges.

FOLLOW UP ACTION:
  • By August 10, 2023 - Submit reports of Charges to be collected on the FY 23-24 tax roll
  to Los Angeles County.

posted agenda pursuant to the Brown Act. The notice of Public Hearing was advertised
May 26, 2023 and June 2, 2023.

Subject: City of Avalon Sewer, Saltwater, and Solid Waste Rate Study Final Report

Dear Mr. Baker:

HDR Engineering, Inc. (HDR) is pleased to present the final report for the sewer, saltwater,
and solid waste rate study update conducted for the City of Avalon (City). The primary
objective in conducting a rate study for each utility is to establish cost-based and proportional
utility rates, for a five-year period, which is intended to provide adequate and sustainable
funding for each utility's operational and capital needs. This report outlines the approach,
methodology, findings, and conclusions of the rate study process undertaken for each utility.

This report was developed utilizing the City's accounting, operating, and historical customer
billing records. HDR has relied upon this information to develop our analyses which formed our
findings, conclusions, and recommendations. At the same time, this study was developed utilizing
generally accepted rate setting principles. The conclusions and recommendations contained
within this report are intended to provide the City with cost-based and equitable utility rates for
its customers.

We appreciate the assistance provided by the City staff, management, and the City Council in the
development of this study.

 I  Executive Summary
Int roduction
HDR Engineering, Inc. {HDR) was retained by the City of Avalon {City) to perform a comprehensive
sewer, saltwater, and solid waste rate study. The development of this study examines the
adequacy of the existing revenues (rates) for each utility and provides the basis for any
recommended adjustments to rates, while seeking to adequately and equitably fund the
operating and capital (O&M) needs of each utility. This report describes the overall methodology
used to analyze the City's rates, for e9ch utility, along with the findings, conclusions, and
recommendations.

Overview of the Rat e Study Process
A sewer, saltwater, and solid waste rate study uses three interrelated analyses to address the
adequacy and equity of a utility's rates. These three analyses are a revenue requirement analysis,
a cost of service analysis, and a rate design analysis. These three analyses are illustrated below
in Figure ES-1.

The results from each of the above tasks, for each utility, were used as the basis for establishing

Key Rate Study Results
Each utility was financially evaluated on a standalone basis. By reviewing the sewer, saltwater,
and solid waste utilities on a standalone basis, the need to adequately fund both O&M and capital
infrastructure must be balanced against the rate impacts to customers and therefore, avoid any
inter-fund subsidies.

 Sewer Cost of Service Analysis
The City's current sewer rate structure was reviewed to determine the cost-basis and the
proportionality of the sewe r rates in the prior study wh ich was completed in 2017 {2017 Study).
It is also important t o note that t he City does not receive metered water use data, which is
typica lly used to estimate the wastewater flow in a sewer cost of service analysis for establishing
rates. Therefore, the first step was to define one (1) equiva lent dwelling unit (EDU), as the base
for estimated sewer flow. The EDU reflects t he estimated flow of the typical single-family
residential customer. In other words, each single-family customer is assigned 1 EDU. The
remaining customers (non-residential) are billed based on a variety of different units such as the
number of rooms, showers, seats, etc., with each billing unit being a proportion of 1 EDU based
on industry standard sewer flow estimates.

The City's cost of service study ana lyzed the proportions based on assumed wastewater
contributions. Given the results of the review of the flow assumptions, and resu lting proportion
of an EDU, the City's rates for non-residential customers appeared to be equitable and
proportiona l. As this ana lysis has been completed recently, this analysis reviewed the ,prior
approach, and it was maintained. It is also important to note that t he customer characteristics
and the industry standard flow assumptions have not changed since the 2017 study. Given this,
proposed sewer rates can be developed to reflect t he overa ll revenue needs and relationships
between the customer types on an EDU basis as is the City's current approach.

2.1 Introduction

2.2 Generally Accepted Rate Setting Principles
As a practical matter, utilities should consider setting their rates around some generally accepted
or global principles and guidelines. Utility rates should be:
•  Cost-based, equitable, and set at a level that meets the utility's full revenue requirement
•  Easy to understand and administer
•  Designed to conform with generally accepted rate setting techniques
•  Stable in their ability to provide adequate revenues for meeting the utility's financial,
  operating, and regulatory requirements
•  Established at a level that is stable from year-to-year from a customer's perspective
•  Established in compliance with State law

2.3 Types of Ut ilit ies
Utilities are generally divided into two types:
1. Public utilities are owned by a city, county, or special district, and are operated at zero profit
Public utilities are capitalized or financed by issuing debt and recovering funds from customers
through direct capital contributions or user rates. Public or municipal utilities are typically exempt
from state and federal income taxes. A publicly elected City Council or Board of Directors usually
regulates public utilities.
2. Private utilities are "for profit" enterprises and are owned by a private company and/or
  shareholders. The shareholders are, in essence, the owners of the private utility. Therefore,
  the owners of a private utility may not be customers or local citizens, but rather numerous
  individuals or shareholders spread across the United States. A private utility is capitalized by
  issuing stock to the general public.

Private utilities are taxable entities. Given their for-profit status, their rates and operations are
generally regulated by a state public utility commission or other regulatory body.

As a point of reference, the City's utilities are public (municipal) utilities and the analyses have
been based on the methodology generally utilized by for public utilities.

 2.4 Determining the Revenue Requ irement
Because public and private utilities have very different administrative and financial
characteristics, their methods differ for determining revenue requirements and setting rates. A
discussion of these rate setting differences are provided below.

2.4.1  Public Utilit ies
Most public utilities use the "cash basis" 1 approach for establishing their revenue requirement
and setting rates. This approach conforms to most public utility budgetary requirements and the
calculation is easy to understand. A public utility:
•  Totals its cash expenditures for a period of time to determine required revenues
•  Adds operation and maintenance {O&M) expenses to any applicable taxes or transfer
  payments to determine total operating expenses. Operation and maintenance expenses
  include the materials, electricity, labor, supplies, etc. needed to keep the utility functioning.
•  Calculates capital costs by adding debt service payments {principal and interest) to capital
  improvements financed with · rate revenues. In lieu of including capital improvements
  financed with rate revenues, a utility sometimes includes depreciation expense to stabilize
  annual revenue requirement.

Under the cash basis approach, the sum of the capital and operating expenses equals the utility's
revenue requirernent during any period of time (see Table 2 - 1).

  Table 2 - 1

  +  O&M Expense  +  O&M Expense
  +  Taxes or Transfer Payments  +  Taxes or Transfer Payments
  +  Capital Improvements Financed with Rate  +  Depreciation Expense
  Revenues (<! Depreciation Exp.)
  +  Debt service (Principal+ Interest)  +  Return on Investment

  =  Total Revenue Requirement  =  Total Revenue Requirement

Note that the two portions of the capital expense component {debt service and capital
improvements financed from rates) are necessary under the cash basis approach because utilities
generally cannot finance all their capital facilities with long-term debt. An exception occurs if a
public utility provides service to a wholesale or contract customer. In this situation, a public utility
cou ld use the "utility basis" approach (see below) to earn a fair return on its investment.

3.2 Determining the Sewer Utility Revenue Requirement
The revenue requirement is the first analytical step in the comprehensive rate study process. This
analysis determines the adequacy of the overall sewer rates, at current rate levels, to recover
sufficient revenues to fund the utility's projected total annual operations and maintenance
expenses and capital-related costs incurred to meet the various aspects of providing the utility's
services. From this analysis, a determination can be made as to the overall level of rate
adjustment needed to provide adequate and prudent funding for both operating and capital
needs.

In developing the revenue requirement, it was assumed the sewer utility must financially "stand
on its own" and be properly funded. As a result, the revenue requirement as developed herein
assumes the full and proper funding needed to operate and maintain the system on a financially
sound and prudent basis. This includes maintaining adequate reserve levels, prudently funding
annual repair and replacement needs (rate-funded capital), and meeting other industry standard
financial metrics (e.g., debt service coverage), where applicable. Provided below is a more
detailed discussion of the de_v elopment of the revenue requirement analysis for the City's sewer
utility.

3.2.1  Determining the Ti me Period and Approach
The first step in calculating the revenue requirement for the sewer utility was to establish a test
period, or the time period to review the revenue requirement analysis. For this study, the
revenue requirement was developed for a projected five-year projected time period of FY 2021-
22 through FY 2025-26 for the projection of sewer rate revenue adjustments. Reviewing a multi-
year time period is recommended in order to more easily identify any major expenses that may
be on the horizon and also help detect any key cost trends that may be occurring. By anticipating
future financial requirements, the City can begin planning for these changes sooner, thereby
minimizing short-term rate impacts and minimizing overall long-term rate volatility.

The second step in determining the revenue requirement was to decide on the basis of
accumulating costs. For the City's sewer revenue requirement analysis, a "cash basis" approach
was utilized. This method is the most commonly used methodology by municipal utilities to set
their revenue requirement. The actual revenue requirement developed for the City was
customized to follow their system of accounts (budget documents). However, the revenue
requirement still contains the basic cost components of a cash basis methodology.

 Rate Funding
A general financial guideline states that, at a minimum, a utility should fund an amount from
rates which is equal to or greater than the annual depreciation expense. Annual depreciation
expense reflects the current investment in plant being depreciated or "losing" its useful life.
Therefore, this portion of plant investment needs to be annually funded to maintain the existing
level of infrastructure. In addition, consideration should be given to using rate revenues to fund
an amount greater than the annual depreciation expense for repairs and replacements as costs
escalate over time and replacement cost is generally greater than the original cost. Whenever
possible, the City should be funding capital projects from rates in an amount greater than annual
depreciation expense to better reflect replacement costs. At the present time, the annual
depreciation expense of the sewer utility is approximately $378,000 based on the City's financial
statements. Over the course of the five-year review period, the City is funding a total of $2.0
million via rates, or an average of $383,000 per year. With the proposed rate funding included
within this study, the sewer utility has made significant strides toward adequate funding for the
repair and replacement of the existing sewer system infrastructure.

Reserve Funding
The use of reserves to fund capital improvements is another method available to the City, when
and if reserves are available. During the projected time period of the rate study, there will be
approximately $462,000 in reserves used as a funding source for capital improvement projects
over the review period. The sewer utility reserve fund has historically been established by annual
surpluses in years where revenues may be greater than the annual expenses of the sewer utility.
This allows the City to reserve funds for projects in later years when more or larger projects are
undertaken. This approach helps to mitigate future rate adjustments and smooth rates over time.
However, close attention should be given to the reserve balance as to not reduce it below the
minimum target.

Long-Term Debt
The use of long-term debt is another potential source of funding for capital projects. There a re
advantages and disadvantages with the issuance of long-term debt and it is important to weigh
them when deciding whether to issue or not. Long-term debt does have prudent applications
whereby it acts as a financial device to spread the costs of a larger project, such as a new pump
station, over multiple years. Doing so then assigns the costs of the new facility to the customers
who are benefit from it over the life of the facility (so called "inter-generational equity"}. For this
study, no additional long-term debt has been assumed.

As can be seen, there are multiple methods by which the City may fund their capital projects.
Each method has an impact upon the revenue requirements of the sewer utility.

3.3 Developme nt of the Sewer Cost of Service
The establishment of cost-based and equitable rates was of paramount importance in the
development of the City's sewer cost of service analysis. Meeting the legal requirements and
documenting the steps taken to meet the requirements, has been in the forefront with the recent
legal challenges in the State of California on utility rates. A focus has been given to meeting the
legal requirements of California Constitution article XIII D, section 6 (A~ticle XIII D). A key
component of Article XII I Dis the development of rates which reflect the cost of providing service
and are proportionally allocated among the various customer classes of service, and the
customers within each class. HDR would point out that there is no single methodology for
equitably assigning costs to the various customer classes. The Water Environment Federation
Manual of Practice #27 provides various methodologies which may be used to establish cost-
based rates. Unfortunately, Article XIII D is not prescriptive and does not provide a specific
methodology for establishing cost-based rates.

HDR is of the opinion that the proposed rates meet the legal requirements of Articl e XIII D. HDR
reaches this conclusion based upon the following:

 •  The revenue derived from sewer rates does not exceed the funds required to provide the
  property related service (i.e., sewer service). The proposed rates are designed to collect the

•  The revenues derived from sewer rates shall not be used for any purpose other than that
  for which the fee or charge is imposed. The revenues derived from the City's sewer rates are

•  The amount of a fee or charge imposed upon a parcel or person as an incident of property
  ownership shall not exceed the proportional costs of the service attributable to the parcel.
  The study has appropriately grouped customers into customer classes of service (residential,
  restaurants, hotel, theatre, etc.) that reflect the varying customer usage patterns and system
  requirements (i.e., the benefits they receive from and burdens they place on the system) of
  each customer class of service. The grouping of customers and rates into these classes of
  service creates the equity and fairness expected under Article XIII D by having differing rates
  by customer classes of service which reflect both the level of revenue to be collected by the
  utility, and the manner in which these costs are incurred and equitably assigned to customer
  classes of service based upon their proportional impacts.

3.3.1  Overview of the City's Current Sewer Rate Structure
As mentioned previously, the cost of service analysis was reviewed for appropriateness given the
recent analysis completed in the 2017 Study. This included a review of the proportionality of the
sewer rates. It is important to note that the City does not have the ability to obtain metered
water consumption data, which is helpful in reviewing and developing an equitable allocation of
costs. Given these limitations and based on the current rate structure used by the City, an
approach was developed to review the proportionality, or cost comparison, of the rate structure.

For the cost comparison, it is assumed that residential customers were charged based on being
assigned 1 EDU for their estimated sewer flow. The calculation of the billing unit for each type of
billing for the non-residential customers is based on the estimated sewer flows resulting from

review the flow assumptions for each billing component of the City's sewer rates. There were

non-residential charges for the City. The estimated flows from each of these sources were used
to determine the proportion of an EDU for each billing component (seats, rooms, etc.). In other
words, the estimated flow for each customer was compared to the estimated residential flow.
This calculation provided a ratio of each customer class to a residential customer. This calculation

•  Rat es which are easy t o understand from the customer' s perspect ive

Given the requirement and intent of Proposition 218, the last consideration, cost-based rates,

 Just as in the sewer capital funding plan, there are numerous funding sources that can be used
to fund the capital projects. Among the methods that may be used to finance these saltwater
capital improvement projects are long-term debt, reserves, and rates. Historically the City has
primarily utilized rates and reserves to fund the capital improvements. As with the sewer utility,
based on the rate transition plan developed as part of this revenue requirement, the City is
projected to have adequate resources to provide funding for these capital projects. Provided
below is a summary of the typical funding sources the City has used, and will continue to use, to
fund the capital improvements over the next five year period.

Rate Funding
A general financial guideline states that, at a minimum, a utility should fund an amount equal to
or greater than annual depreciation through rates. Annual depreciation expense reflects the
current investment in saltwater plant being depreciated or "losing" its useful life. Therefore, this
portion of plant investment needs to be replaced to maintain the existing level of infrastructure.
While the general financial guideline suggests funding an amount at least equal to the
depreciation expense, consideration should also be given to funding within rates some amount
greater than the annual depreciation expense to reflect the cost of replacement. The
depreciation expense reflects the cost of infrastructure that was constructed, on average, 15 to
20 years ago. Funding for the replacement cost is prudent and minimizes costs/rates over time.
With that in mind, for this review period, the City has increased the level of rate funding for their
renewal and replacement projects. The City has increased the annual rate funding for capital
projects from $65,000 in FY 2020-21 to $185,000 by FY 2025-26. As a point of reference, the City's
current annual depreciation expense for the saltwater system is approximately $55,000 as
provided in the City's financial records for FY 2019-20. Given that, this study has greatly improved
the funding for renewal and replacement capital projects but is not at a level of funding for full
replacement cost.

Reserve Funding
Available reserve funds are another method of funding capital improvements. For the study,
there are no assumed uses of reserves as a funding source for capital improvement projects. This
reserve fund is typically funded by annual surpluses, just as in the sewer utility. Again, this allows
the City to reserve funds for projects in later years when more or larger projects are undertaken.
This approach helps to mitigate future rate adjustments and smooth rates over time. Over the
planning horizon, close attention should be given to the reserve balance as to not reduce fund
balances below minimum targets described below.

Long-Term Debt
Another potential funding source for capital projects is the issuance of long-term debt. While
there are certain advantages and disadvantages with the issuance of long-term debt, it is
important to weigh all of them when deciding whether to issue or not. Long-term debt is typically
not issued to fund renewal and replacement projects similar to those being proposed during this
time period. Rather, long-term debt is often issued for major capital projects which have an
immediate impact on rates and long-term debt is a financing mechanism to smoothly
finance/fund the major capital project. For this analysis, no new long-term debt is assumed ov~r
the planning period.

21 adopted operating budget, and capital improvement plan. The following sections provide a
detailed discussion of the analytical steps and key assumptions contained in the development of
the projections of the City's solid waste revenues and expenses.

5.2.2  Projection of Solid Waste Revenues
The City receives revenue from two primary sources, rate revenue and miscellaneous revenue.
The solid waste rate revenues are based on the current rate structure and collected on an annual
basis, in the same manner as the sewer and saltwater utilities. Other miscellaneous revenue
includes items such as construction debris, grease removal, and other various revenues.

The first step in developing the revenue requirement was to develop a projection of solid waste
rate revenues, at present rate levels, which was taken from the City's FY 2020-21 budget. In total,
using the present solid waste rates, the City is projected to receive approximately $1.8 million
annually in rate revenues in FY 2020-21 through FY 2025-26 based on flat annual customer
growth

On a combined basis, considering the rate revenues along with miscellaneous revenues, the City's
total projected solid waste revenues are expected to be approximately $2.0 million annua lly
through FY 2025-26. Exhibit 3 of Technical Appendix C provides the detail of the various sources
of revenues for the City's Solid Waste utility.

5.2.3  Proj ection of Solid Wa st e Operation and M aintenance Expe nses
Operation and maintenance (O&M) expenses are incurred by the City to operate and maintain
the solid waste system. The costs incurred in this area are expensed during the current year and
are not capitalized or depreciated. In general, O&M expenses are grouped into functional
categories. To begin the process of projecting O&M expenses over the planning horizon,
escalation factors were developed. Escalation factors were developed for the basic types of
expenses incurred: salaries, benefits, materials and supplies, utilities, equipment, and
miscellaneous expenses. Escalation factors were projected based on historic inflationary trends
and assumed to be approximately 1.5% - 5.0% per year. These escalation factors are consistent
with those used in the sewer and saltwater revenue requirement analyses. The escalation factors
used in the projection of O&M expenses can be found in Exhibit 2 of Technical Appendix C in
detail.

Given the adopted budget for FY 2020-21 O&M expenses, the O&M expenses were escalated
based on the previously mentioned escalation factors. The total operation and maintenance
expenses are projected to be approximately $2.0 million in FY 2020-21. The City's solid waste
O&M expenses are projected to increase to approximately $2.7 million by FY 2025-26 as a result
of assumed inflation over the time period. Additionally, starting in FY 2021-22 and continuing
through FY 2023-24, the City is anticipated to spend $100,000 annually for landfill expansion over
and abov FY 2020-21 budget levels. In addition, additional labor costs are included in FY 2021-22
to reflect historical staffing levels. The City was also recently notified that the cost of the
sanitation contract wou ld be increasing due to unfunded mandates recently enacted by the
State. The projection of O&M expenses can be found in Exhibit 3 ofTechnical Appendix C in detail.

5.2.4  Project ion of Solid W aste Capital Improvement Project s and Funding
At this time, the City's solid waste utility does not have any planned annual capital improvements
over the review period. This is primarily due to the fact that the City contract's the solid waste
collection and disposal services. This means that the City does not have the financial burden of
maintaining the equipment for solid waste collection and transportation. Although there are no
capital projects during the review period, the City will continue to be in a financial position that
allows them the flexibility to fund future capital needs if necessary.

5.2.5  Projection of Taxes and Transfer Payments
As with the City's sewer and sa ltwater utility, there were no taxes paid or transfers identified for
the solid waste utility over the review period.

5.3 Development of the Solid Waste Cost of Service
Just as with the sewer and saltwater, the cost of service analysis developed in the 2017 Study
and the assumptions were reviewed as part of this study. It is important to note, the City
contracts for solid waste collection and disposal services. Consequently, the City does not have
information available on customers in regards to the size of the solid waste container or the
number of pick-ups. Given this, the information necessary to identify the cost components
related to providing service to various types of customers is unavailable. It should also be noted
that information on actual waste generation by customer type is limited, as most collection and
disposal practices do not separate by customer type. For example, a utility typically does not have
information on the average tonnage collected from an individual restaurant or grocery store. At
best, some utilities may have total tonnage collected by residential or commercial in aggregate.

The City' s solid waste rate structure is further complicated by the fact that a customer may not
have a specified, or individual, solid waste disposal container. In many cases, multiple customers
dispose of their waste in a single solid waste disposal container. As such, the solid waste
contractor may collect waste multiple times a week, or even multiple times a day depending, on
the need and activities in the area. Given this, it is difficult, if not impossible, to determine those
customers that benefit from a specific container or need at the current time. As a result, the
ratios utilized in the 2017 study were maintained as they are based on estimates of waste
generation by customer type.

5.6 Rate Adoption
Proposition 218 outlines a specific process to legally adopt and implement the proposed sewer,
sa ltwater, and solid waste rates. The first requirement is that the rates must be cost-based and
proportional, which is the purpose of completing the rate study. Once the proposed sewer,
saltwater, and solid waste rates have been developed, a public process must be undertaken to
adopt the proposed rates. This began with the presentation of the proposed rates to the Avalon
City Council in April 2021. At this meeting, the City Council directed staff to mail the Proposition
218 notices -shown in the Proposition 218 Appendix- to the City's customers which outlines the
proposed changes in rates. The notice also contains the time, date, and location of the public
hearing, which is shown in the Approved Notice Appendix. The City Council then held a public
hearing on June 1, 2021 to discuss the publicly noticed and proposed rates. Absent sufficient
written protest by customers, the City Council moved to adopt the proposed sewer, saltwater,
and solid waste rates as outlined in the customer notification over the next five-year period.

REPORT SUMMARY: With limited exceptions, for more than 30 years , a singular waterfront
business has been contracted by the City for both the annual installation, maintenance and
operation of the End Float located at the end of the City's float at the base of the Green Pleasure
Pier, and the semi-exclusive shore boat franchise agreement.

On March 15, 2017, the City of Avalon (City) entered into a five-year Semi-Exclusive Shore Boat
Franchise and Shore Boat Services Provider Agreement (hereafter "Shore Boat Agreement")
with Catalina Coastal Tours, LLC dba Catalina Coastal Tours and Fishing. The Agreement
established specific hours of operation, a fee schedule, and annual $239,000 subsidy provided
from the City to the Contractor in monthly installments. The Agreement also included two 5 year
renewal terms, but only guaranteed the subsidy for the initial 5-year term.

On December 4, 2018, the City Council authorized the release of a request for proposals for
qualified waterside business parties to contract to build and operate an end float for exclusive
use at the base of the City-owned float at the end of the Green Pleasure Pier. Only one proposal
was received by the January 2019 deadline. On March 19, 2019 the City Council waived all
irregularities and awarded a contract to Catalina Island Coastal Tours and Fishing for the building
and operating of the End Float.

As outlined in the March 19, 2019 Staff Report regarding the End Float Award: "The main criteria
for evaluation and the impetus for the solicitation of the End Float was to alleviate congestion
within the harbor, which Staff believes would be accomplished if the lease is awarded to Catalina
Island Coastal Tours & Fishing. They currently hold the Semi-Exclusive Shore Boat Franchise
and Shore Boat Services Provider Agreement with the City. They propose to operate both the
Shore Boat operations and their fishing charters off of this End Float, opening up the existing
docks experiencing congestion currently."
 In March 2021 , the City Council approve an amendment to the Shore Boat Ag reement with
Catalina Coastal Tours granting a 5-year renewal term , increasing the fee schedule, and
increasing the annual subsidy by $50,000 (approximately 20%) to $289,000.

Recently, the principal operator from Catalina Coastal Tours indicated their desire to assign the
remaining term of the Shore Boat Agreement to Catalina Coastal Shoreboat Services, LLC. An
introductory letter was received on April ·10, 2023 from Catalina Coastal Shoreboat Services,
LLC outlining their qualifications and interest in the assignment.

Concerns exist regarding the assignment of the remainder of the Shore Boat Agreement. Most
significantly, it is unclear how the assignment will impact congestion in Avalon Harbor. With
current dock loads, the Harbormaster has indicated adding shore boat operations to City-owned
floats will not be possible. Having two different entities control the Shore Boat Agreement and
the End Float Lease may not be in the best interests of the City.

Further, though the proposed assignee has visited Avalon Harbor to observe operations, they
have no history as waterside permit holders,

The City Council has three potential actions it may consider regarding this assignment request:
  1. Deny the request.
  2. Request more information from Catalina Coastal Tours and Catalina Coastal Shoreboat
  Services regarding the assignment and continuity of operations.
  3. Allow the assignment on a trial basis with conditions to guarantee managerial and
  operational consistency.
  4. Allow the assignment without conditions.

GOAL ALIGNMENT: Not aligned.

FISCAL IMPACTS: There will be no change to the budgeted sum through the remaining term
of the contract.
